claim: Life expectancy has risen sharply in the last 50 years.
source_text: Life expectancy has risen sharply in the last 50 years.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about global health trends.

claim: The Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics model can be applied to demonstrate a mathematical relationship of income to childhood and adult survival.
source_text: We applied the classic Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics to demonstrate a novel mathematical relationship of income to childhood (aged 0–5 years) and adult (aged 15–60 years) survival.
evidence_reasoning: The authors present their novel application of the MM model to mortality data from 180 countries, demonstrating this relationship through empirical analysis.

claim: Maximum child and adult survival rose by about 1% per year from 1970 to 2007.
source_text: Maximum child and adult survival rose by about 1% per year.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative finding derived from the authors' analysis of mortality data across the study period.

claim: Critical incomes fell by half for children from 1970 to 2007.
source_text: Critical incomes fell by half for children
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative result from the authors' MM model analysis of child mortality data.

claim: Critical incomes doubled for men from 1970 to 2007.
source_text: Critical incomes fell by half for children, but doubled for men.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative result from the authors' MM model analysis of adult male mortality data.

claim: HIV infection and smoking account for some, but not all, of the rising critical incomes for adult survival.
source_text: HIV infection and smoking account for some, but not all, of the rising critical incomes for adult survival.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on the authors' covariate analysis showing partial but incomplete explanation of the observed trends.

claim: Global life expectancy rose by about 90 days per year in the 20th century.
source_text: In the 20th century, global life expectancy rose by about 90 days per year
evidence_reasoning: This statement references established findings from Oeppen (2002) and Vallin and Meslé (2009).

claim: Much of the increase in global life expectancy in the 20th century was driven by substantial declines in childhood mortality.
source_text: global life expectancy rose by about 90 days per year, with much of that increase driven by substantial declines in childhood mortality
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by references to Oeppen (2002) and Vallin and Meslé (2009).

claim: In most low-income countries, death in middle age is increasing in relative importance as other causes decrease and the effects of smoking increase.
source_text: In most low-income countries, death in middle age is increasing in relative importance as other causes decrease and the effects of smoking increase
evidence_reasoning: This statement is supported by citation to Jha (2009).

claim: Most adult deaths are due to noncommunicable diseases, such as vascular, respiratory, or neoplastic diseases, with a significant minority due to HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis.
source_text: Most adult deaths are due to noncommunicable diseases, such as vascular, respiratory, or neoplastic diseases, with a significant minority due to HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Beaglehole et al. (2011b).

claim: Preston characterized the relationship between life expectancy at birth and gross domestic product per capita as a logistic function.
source_text: Preston, originally, characterized the relationship between life expectancy (e0) at birth and gross domestic product per capita ('GDP') as a logistic function
evidence_reasoning: This references Preston's (1975) original work on the Preston curve.

claim: The Preston curve showed an upward shift between the years 1960 and 2000.
source_text: Figure 1A is a reproduced plot of the original 'Preston curve', with an upward shift between the years 1960 and 2000
evidence_reasoning: This is based on Preston's (1975) published findings.

claim: The Michaelis-Menten mathematical model was first described in 1913.
source_text: The Michaelis–Menten mathematical model first described in 1913
evidence_reasoning: This is established historical fact about the MM model, cited to Michaelis and Menten (1913).

claim: The Michaelis-Menten model was initially developed to analyze enzyme kinetics.
source_text: The Michaelis–Menten mathematical model first described in 1913 (Michaelis and Menten, 1913) was initially developed to analyze enzyme kinetics.
evidence_reasoning: This is established scientific knowledge about the original purpose of the MM model.

claim: Enzymes are biomacromolecules that act as catalysts, agents that accelerate the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.
source_text: Enzymes are biomacromolecules that act as catalysts, agents that accelerate the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.
evidence_reasoning: This is fundamental biochemical knowledge about enzyme function.

claim: Critical income is defined as the level of daily income associated with the achievement of 50% of the maximum life expectancy.
source_text: This construct is defined as the level of daily income associated with the achievement of 50% of the maximum life expectancy
evidence_reasoning: This is a novel definition introduced by the authors based on their adaptation of the MM model.

claim: Maximum life expectancy approximates the observed average life expectancy in high-income countries.
source_text: 'maximum life expectancy' is empiric, approximating the observed average life expectancy in high-income countries
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' methodological approach, supported by reference to Rodgers (2002).

claim: Two times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7% of the maximal life expectancy.
source_text: two, four, and nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7%, 80%, and 90% of the maximal life expectancy, respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mathematical property derived from the MM equation structure.

claim: Four times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 80% of the maximal life expectancy.
source_text: two, four, and nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7%, 80%, and 90% of the maximal life expectancy, respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mathematical property derived from the MM equation structure.

claim: Nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 90% of the maximal life expectancy.
source_text: two, four, and nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7%, 80%, and 90% of the maximal life expectancy, respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mathematical property derived from the MM equation structure.

claim: The fits of the logistic, log-linear, and Michaelis-Menten models were comparable for life expectancy data.
source_text: Although the fits of the models were comparable, the parameters of the logistic and log-linear models have less obvious explanatory value.
evidence_reasoning: This is based on the authors' comparative analysis of model fits shown in Table 2.

claim: The parameters of the logistic and log-linear models have less obvious explanatory value than the Michaelis-Menten model.
source_text: the parameters of the logistic and log-linear models have less obvious explanatory value.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretive conclusion based on their analysis of model parameters.

claim: All inflection points for the logistic function were determined to be negative (from −$2.69 in 1970 to −$8.47 in 2007).
source_text: For the logistic function, all inflection points were determined to be negative (from −$2.69 in 1970 to −$8.47 in 2007)
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' analysis of the logistic model.

claim: Negative inflection points are impossible income values for any country.
source_text: all inflection points were determined to be negative (from −$2.69 in 1970 to −$8.47 in 2007) and are impossible income values for any country.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical statement based on the fact that income cannot be negative.

claim: The logistic function is overly complex and not necessary to model the data.
source_text: This suggests that the logistic function is overly complex and not necessary to model the data.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation based on the negative inflection points finding.

claim: For each year, the maximum life expectancy approximated the 5% trimmed mean life expectancy observed in countries with annual incomes greater than $12,276.
source_text: For each year, the maximum life expectancy approximated the 5% trimmed mean life expectancy observed in countries with annual incomes greater than $12,276 (t(8) = −1.596, p=0.149, not statistically significant; Table 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is a validation finding from the authors' statistical analysis.

claim: Maximum life expectancy and critical income parameters were not sensitive to the random removal of 5% of the data.
source_text: we performed a sensitivity analysis on the maximum life expectancy and critical income parameters and determined that both were not sensitive to the random removal of 5% of the data
evidence_reasoning: This is a result from the authors' sensitivity analysis with specific statistical tests reported.

claim: The maximal life expectancy rose from 67.8 years (95% uncertainty interval 65.4–70.1 years) in 1970 to 75.5 years (95% uncertainty interval 73.9–77.1 years) in 2007.
source_text: The maximal life expectancy rose from 67.8 years (95% uncertainty interval 65.4–70.1 years) in 1970 to 75.5 years (95% uncertainty interval 73.9–77.1 years) in 2007.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative finding from the authors' MM model analysis.

claim: The change in maximal life expectancy represents a linear increase of 75 (95% uncertainty interval 48–99 years) days per calendar year over the last 40 years.
source_text: This change in maximal life expectancy represents a linear increase of 75 (95% uncertainty interval 48–99 years) days per calendar year (R2 = 0.875) over the last 40 years
evidence_reasoning: This is a calculated rate of change from the authors' analysis with statistical fit reported.

claim: The increase of 75 days per calendar year in maximal life expectancy is comparable to the life expectancy increase of almost 90 days per calendar year for the 20th century.
source_text: and is comparable to the life expectancy increase of almost 90 days per calendar year for the 20th century
evidence_reasoning: This compares the authors' finding to established results from Oeppen (2002).

claim: The critical income needed to achieve half of maximal overall life expectancy declined from $1.48 ($1.18–$1.78) in 1970 to $1.21 ($0.98–$1.44) in 2007.
source_text: The critical income (in constant 2005 international dollars) needed to achieve half of maximal overall life expectancy declined from $1.48 ($1.18–$1.78) in 1970 to $1.21 ($0.98–$1.44) in 2007
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative finding from the authors' MM model analysis.

claim: The critical income of $1.21 in 2007 is equivalent to the extreme poverty line of $1.25 per day.
source_text: equivalent in 2007 to the extreme poverty line of $1.25 per day
evidence_reasoning: This references the established World Bank extreme poverty line definition.

claim: The decline in critical income from 1970 to 2007 represents an 18% decrease in critical income to gain almost 4 additional years of life expectancy.
source_text: this represents an 18% decrease in critical income to gain almost 4 additional years of life expectancy.
evidence_reasoning: This is a calculated percentage change from the authors' findings.

claim: Critical income declined linearly at a rate of −$0.09 per decade (−$0.06 to −$0.13, R2 = 0.839).
source_text: Critical income declined linearly at a rate of −$0.09 per decade (−$0.06 to −$0.13, R2 = 0.839).
evidence_reasoning: This is a calculated rate of change from the authors' regression analysis.

claim: Maximum survival for all age groups rose at statistically the same rate between 1970 and 2007.
source_text: Maximum survival for all age groups rose at statistically the same rate between 1970 and 2007
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from the authors' comparative statistical analysis across age groups.

claim: Critical incomes diverged dramatically for children and adults from 1970 to 2007.
source_text: However, critical incomes diverged dramatically for children and adults
evidence_reasoning: This is a key finding from the authors' analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: From 1970 to 1980, the critical income values for children, adult males, and adult females were statistically equivalent, between $0.54–$0.58 per day.
source_text: From 1970 to 1980, the critical income values for children, adult males, and adult females were statistically equivalent, between $0.54–$0.58 per day.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' analysis of early time period data.

claim: The critical income for child survival fell by over half from $0.58 ($0.46–$0.70) in 1970 to $0.24 ($0.20–$0.28) in 2010.
source_text: Over the 40-year period from 1970 to 2010, the critical income for child survival fell by over half from $0.58 ($0.46–$0.70) to $0.24 ($0.20–$0.28).
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative finding from the authors' MM model analysis for children.

claim: Critical income more than doubled for adult male survival from $0.54 ($0.38–$0.71) in 1970 to $1.20 ($0.81–$1.58) in 2010.
source_text: critical income more than doubled for adult male survival from $0.54 ($0.38–$0.71) to $1.20 ($0.81–$1.58)
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative finding from the authors' MM model analysis for adult males.

claim: Critical income rose over 50% for adult female survival from $0.57 ($0.43–$0.70) in 1970 to $0.89 ($0.65–$1.12) in 2010.
source_text: rose over 50% for adult female survival from $0.57 ($0.43–$0.70) to $0.89 ($0.65–$1.12)
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific quantitative finding from the authors' MM model analysis for adult females.

claim: The 1970 and 2007 survival curves for adult men crossed over at a value of $10.95 GDP per capita per day.
source_text: The 1970 and 2007 survival curves for adult men crossed over at a value for $10.95 GDP per capita per day.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' analysis of the intersection of survival curves.

claim: There are 58 countries with a total adult male population of approximately 780 million (or 35% of the world adult male population) below the income value of $10.95 per day.
source_text: There are 58 countries with a total adult male population of approximately 780 million (or 35% of the world adult male population) below this income value.
evidence_reasoning: This is a demographic calculation based on the authors' analysis and population data.

claim: For countries below $10.95 per day income, adult male survival was lower in 2007 than in 1970.
source_text: For these countries, adult male survival was lower in 2007 than in 1970
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of survival curve crossover implications.

claim: The 1970 and 2007 survival curves for adult women crossed over at $5.93 GDP per capita per day.
source_text: Adult male (A) and female (B) survival regression curves for the years 1970 and 2007. Adult survival in 2007 is lower than in 1970 for countries under the income threshold of $10.95 (for men) and $5.93 (for women).
evidence_reasoning: This is stated in the figure caption and represents a finding from the authors' analysis.

claim: Adjusting for HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption reduced the critical income for adult males in 2000 from $1.20 to $0.70.
source_text: adjusting for HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption reduced the critical income for adult males in 2000 from $1.20 to $0.70
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' covariate analysis.

claim: Adjusting for HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption reduced the critical income for adult females in 2000 from $0.89 to $0.60.
source_text: adjusting for HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption reduced the critical income for adult females in 2000 from $0.89 to $0.60
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' covariate analysis.

claim: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a rise of one cigarette consumed per day per person led to a $1.70 ($0.96–$2.43) increase in critical income for adult men.
source_text: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a rise of one cigarette consumed per day per person and 1% in HIV prevalence led, for adult men, to a $1.70 ($0.96–$2.43) and $0.70 ($0.27–$1.13) increase in critical income, respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' first differences analysis.

claim: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a 1% rise in HIV prevalence led to a $0.70 ($0.27–$1.13) increase in critical income for adult men.
source_text: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a rise of one cigarette consumed per day per person and 1% in HIV prevalence led, for adult men, to a $1.70 ($0.96–$2.43) and $0.70 ($0.27–$1.13) increase in critical income, respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' first differences analysis.

claim: For adult females, a 1% rise in HIV prevalence was associated with a $0.40 ($0.31–$0.49) increase in critical income.
source_text: For adult females, the impact of a 1% rise in HIV prevalence per capita was associated with a $0.40 ($0.31–$0.49) increase in critical income
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' first differences analysis.

claim: For adult females, the impact of smoking was lower, with a change of $0.38 ($0.23–$0.54) per cigarette consumed per day per person.
source_text: however, the impact of smoking was lower, with a change of $0.38 ($0.23–$0.54).
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' first differences analysis.

claim: Adding a covariate for HIV prevalence improved the goodness of fit dramatically for all years and genders.
source_text: Moreover, adding a covariate for HIV prevalence also improved the goodness of fit dramatically for all years and genders
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from the authors' statistical model comparison shown in Table 3.

claim: Child survival replicates the upward and lateral trend in the original Preston curve for life expectancy.
source_text: Unlike for adults, child survival replicates the upward and lateral trend in the original Preston curve for life expectancy.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings comparing child and adult survival trends.

claim: For low- and middle-income countries, the majority of the past gains in life expectancy have been achieved via declining child mortality.
source_text: This suggests that for low- and middle-income countries, the majority of the past gains in life expectancy have been achieved via declining child mortality.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation based on their findings about child survival trends.

claim: The greatest decline in child critical income was achieved after 1990.
source_text: The greatest decline in child critical income was achieved after 1990
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from the authors' analysis of temporal trends in child critical income.

claim: The greatest decline in child critical income after 1990 coincides with actions following the UN's World Summit for Children.
source_text: The greatest decline in child critical income was achieved after 1990, coinciding with actions following the UN's World Summit for Children.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation linking their temporal finding to a known policy event.

claim: Cost-effective interventions have been disproportionately devoted to child and maternal health.
source_text: With justification, cost-effective interventions have been disproportionately devoted to child and maternal health
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Daar et al. (2007).

claim: Increasing coverage of inexpensive health interventions such as immunization, insecticide-treated nets, and case management of childhood infections could be contributing to the decline in critical income for child survival.
source_text: Increasing coverage of inexpensive health interventions such as immunization, insecticide-treated nets, and case management of childhood infections could be contributing to the decline in critical income for child survival
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative explanation for the observed trends, supported by citations to Jamison et al. (2006) and Mathers et al. (2008).

claim: There might be complementary benefits of education in reducing child mortality.
source_text: Moreover, there might be complementary benefits of education in reducing child mortality
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Gakidou et al. (2010).

claim: The achievement of the UN MDG 4 (to reduce child mortality by two-thirds from 1990 levels) might be due to the falling levels of income needed to increase child survival.
source_text: our results imply that the achievement of the UN MDG 4 (to reduce child mortality by two-thirds from 1990 levels) might be due to the falling levels of income needed to increase child survival.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of the policy implications of their findings.

claim: For adult survival, there is a reversal of fortune compared to child survival.
source_text: For adult survival, however, there is a reversal of fortune.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' characterization of their findings showing opposite trends for adults versus children.

claim: Achievable adult survival rates have improved from 1970 to 2007.
source_text: While achievable adult survival rates have improved
evidence_reasoning: This refers to the finding that maximum adult survival increased over the study period.

claim: Improvements in adult survival are only associated with those countries at higher income levels.
source_text: improvements are only associated with those countries at higher income levels.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of the rising critical income for adults.

claim: The rise in critical income suggests that the marginal costs of increasing adult longevity are rising.
source_text: The rise in critical income suggests that the marginal costs of increasing adult longevity are rising
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' economic interpretation of the rising critical income trend.

claim: The rise in critical income may explain the lower rate of decline in adult mortality in countries with low income.
source_text: this may explain the lower rate of decline in adult mortality in countries with low income
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation linking their findings to observations from Rajaratnam et al. (2010).

claim: The emergence of HIV/AIDS in the 1980s and the rise in global smoking prevalence in low- and middle-income countries can explain much, but not the entire rise in critical income for adult males.
source_text: The emergence of HIV/AIDS in the 1980s and the rise in global smoking prevalence in low- and middle-income countries (Guindon and Boisclair, 2003) can explain much, but not the entire rise in critical income for adult males.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' conclusion from their covariate analysis showing partial explanation.

claim: For males, the rise in smoking accounts for over 40% more of the variance in critical income compared to 30% for HIV/AIDS.
source_text: For males, the rise in smoking accounts for over 40% more of the variance in critical income compared to 30% for HIV/AIDS.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' variance analysis of the two covariates.

claim: For adult women, the impact of cigarettes on critical income is much lower than for men.
source_text: For adult women, the impact of cigarettes on critical income is much lower
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from the authors' gender-stratified covariate analysis.

claim: The lower impact of cigarettes on critical income for women reflects the five times lower prevalence of smoking among women compared to men.
source_text: which reflects the five times lower prevalence of smoking among women compared to men
evidence_reasoning: This explanation is supported by citation to Guindon and Boisclair (2003).

claim: Even low levels (4%) of HIV prevalence in rural Tanzania can increase overall adult mortality by more than 50%.
source_text: Even low levels (4%) of HIV prevalence in rural Tanzania can increase overall adult mortality by more than 50%
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Todd et al. (1997).

claim: Smoking increases critical income but has no statistical impact on maximum survival.
source_text: Our findings also show that smoking increases critical income but has no statistical impact on maximum survival.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' covariate analysis.

claim: Prevalence of smoking (and subsequently the deaths attributed to smoking) are rising in low- and middle-income countries but declining in high-income countries.
source_text: This is in line with trends in global smoking, where prevalence of smoking (and subsequently the deaths attributed to smoking) are rising in low- and middle-income countries but declining in high-income countries
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Jha (2009).

claim: An approximate national income per capita of $2.20 per day would be required in 2007 to attain the same achievable adult male survival rate with $1.25 per day in 1970.
source_text: Under the current conditions, an approximate national income per capita of $2.20 per day would be required in 2007 to attain the same achievable adult male survival rate with $1.25 per day in 1970.
evidence_reasoning: This is a calculated comparison from the authors' MM model results.

claim: Should the critical income costs for adults continue to rise (in line with current trends), survival rates for low- and middle-income countries might well deteriorate into the future.
source_text: Moreover, should the critical income costs for adults continue to rise (in line with current trends), survival rates for low- and middle-income countries might well deteriorate into the future.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative projection based on extrapolation of observed trends.

claim: High-income countries have benefited from the rise in maximum survival among adults.
source_text: In contrast, high-income countries have benefited from the rise in maximum survival among adults.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings about maximum survival increases.

claim: The benefit to high-income countries is likely due to more widespread availability of secondary treatments for chronic diseases, most notably for vascular disease, and in particular from sharp reductions in smoking.
source_text: This is likely due to more widespread availability of secondary treatments for chronic diseases, most notably for vascular disease, and in particular from sharp reductions in smoking
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation supported by citation to Jha (2009).

claim: The probabilities of premature adult deaths before the age of 70 from vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases are remarkably similar in low-, middle-, and high-income countries.
source_text: The probabilities of premature adult deaths before the age of 70 from vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases are remarkably similar in low-, middle-, countries and high-income countries
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Strong et al. (2005).

claim: Low-cost, effective, and feasible interventions exist against vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases.
source_text: Low-cost, effective, and feasible interventions (Jha et al., 2002) exist against these diseases
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Jha et al. (2002).

claim: Tobacco control is the most important intervention against vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases.
source_text: most importantly tobacco control
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Jha (2009).

claim: Increased reduction in hazardous alcohol intake (particularly in former Soviet states) is an effective intervention for adult chronic diseases.
source_text: but also increased reduction in hazardous alcohol intake (particularly in former Soviet states; Zaridze et al., 2009)

claim: Low-cost drugs for secondary management of existing disease are effective interventions for adult chronic diseases.
source_text: and low-cost drugs for secondary management of existing disease.

claim: These interventions are still not widely used in low-income countries.
source_text: However, these interventions are still not widely used in low-income countries

claim: Over the past few decades, research and development of new technologies (drugs, vaccines, and policies) have focused mostly on childhood and infectious disease, with fewer worldwide investments for adult chronic diseases.
source_text: Over the past few decades, research and development of new technologies (drugs, vaccines, and policies) have focused mostly on childhood and infectious disease, with fewer worldwide investments for adult chronic diseases

claim: The longer-term trajectory of critical incomes for adult survival might well depend on the development of newer interventions, as well as more widespread application of interventions already proven to be cost effective.

claim: This is the first application of enzyme kinetics to mortality changes.
source_text: This is, as far as we know, the first application of enzyme kinetics to mortality changes.

claim: Since its initial formulation in 1913, the MM equation has been sufficiently adaptable to explain various levels of biological complexity from thousands of single enzyme reactions.

claim: The MM equation has been applied to reversible and quasi-steady state systems.

claim: The MM equation has been applied to the growth of microbial cultures on a nutrient substrate.
source_text: the growth of microbial cultures on a nutrient substrate

claim: The MM equation has been applied to the growth in size of a variety of different animal species.
source_text: the growth in size of a variety of different animal species

claim: The MM equation has been applied to the ability of organisms to acclimate to changes in environmental conditions.

claim: None of the models (log-linear, logistic, MM) can directly elucidate the mechanism(s) that converts income into better survival.
source_text: But none of the models can directly elucidate the mechanism(s) that converts income into better survival.

claim: The MM method allows modeling income as a substrate that catalyzes further changes that more directly impact survival.
source_text: The novel insight from the MM method is that we can model income as a substrate that catalyzes further changes that more directly impact survival.

claim: The median national spending on health is 5% of the GDP.
source_text: the median national spending on health is 5% of the GDP

claim: The United States spends about 18% of GDP on health, representing an outlier.
source_text: and the United States at about 18% of GDP represents an outlier

claim: National income is quite large in relation to health spending for most countries.
source_text: National income is quite large in relation to health spending for most countries

claim: Income directly enables certain technologies, immunization programs, epidemiological knowledge, education, and sanitation systems and other areas, which may themselves be interpreted as 'catalysts'.
source_text: We also reason that income directly enables certain technologies, immunization programs, epidemiological knowledge, education, and sanitation systems and other areas, which may themselves be interpreted as 'catalysts'

claim: The MM method advances understanding of mechanisms by defining critical income levels that measure the efficiency of particular countries using available income to keep up with maximal achievable survival.

claim: The obvious impacts of two large risk factors (HIV and tobacco) on adult survival suggest some mechanistic insights between income and survival.
source_text: Additionally, the obvious impacts of two large risk factors (HIV and tobacco) on adult survival suggest some mechanistic insights between income and survival

claim: Male survival was more unequal from greater male smoking.

evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the differential impact of smoking on male versus female critical income.

claim: Female and male survival were affected equally by the more even spread of HIV infection.
source_text: and female and male survival were affected equally by the more even spread of HIV infection
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the similar impact of HIV on both male and female critical income.

evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' acknowledgment of the need for further research.

source_text: For example, the Monod equation (an adaptation of the MM equation to fit the growth of bacterial cultures; Monod, 1949), which was first proposed in 1949

source_text: was only interpreted thermodynamically 50 years later

source_text: Nonetheless, this equation was (and continues to be) used extensively in the pharmaceutical and food industries as well as in waste treatment systems.

claim: The analyses could be considerably strengthened by examining trends in age, gender, and cause-specific mortality.
source_text: Additionally, our analyses could be considerably strengthened by examining trends in age, gender, and cause-specific mortality
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' acknowledgment of how their work could be improved.

claim: Cause-specific mortality data are simply unavailable for most countries.
source_text: but cause-specific mortality data are simply unavailable for most countries
evidence_reasoning: This is a known limitation in global health data availability.

claim: Less than 3% of all child deaths worldwide were certified according to cause of death.
source_text: for instance, notwithstanding global efforts to identify data for child mortality, less than 3% of all child deaths worldwide were certified according to cause of death
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Liu et al. (2012).

claim: Expanded efforts to measure causes of death is a big global priority.
source_text: Indeed, expanded efforts to measure causes of death is a big global priority
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to Jha (2012) and Vogel (2012).

claim: The development of new physically or biologically inspired analytical models can help elucidate better understanding of global mortality trends.
source_text: and the development of new physically or biologically inspired analytical models can help elucidate better understanding of global mortality trends.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' conclusion about the value of their methodological approach.

claim: Data for 180 countries at 5-year intervals from 1970 to 2007 were included in the analysis.
source_text: Data for 180 countries at 5-year intervals from 1970 to 2007 were included in the analysis
evidence_reasoning: This describes the scope of the dataset used in the study.

claim: Income is defined as per those from the World Bank.
source_text: with definitions of income as per those from the World Bank
evidence_reasoning: This describes the data source for income definitions.

claim: A nonlinear regression analysis (using iterative parameter estimation algorithms) was used to calculate the parameters for the Michaelis-Menten adapted model and the logistic model.
source_text: For the Michaelis–Menten adapted model and the logistic model, a nonlinear regression analysis (using iterative parameter estimation algorithms; Greco and Hakala, 1979) was used to calculate the parameters.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the statistical method used in the analysis.

claim: Countries with missing mortality or income estimates were eliminated from the regression analysis on a year-by-year basis.
source_text: Countries with missing mortality or income estimates were eliminated from the regression analysis on a year-by-year basis.
evidence_reasoning: This describes how missing data were handled in the analysis.

claim: Analysis for the year 2000 was restricted to countries with complete data for both HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption (n = 86).
source_text: For the year 2000, analysis was restricted to countries with complete data for both HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption (n = 86).
evidence_reasoning: This describes a specific data restriction in the covariate analysis.

claim: SPSS (version 19) was used to conduct all regression analyses.
source_text: We used SPSS (version 19) to conduct all regression analyses.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the software used for statistical analysis.

claim: Altering the future cost curve for adult survival will require more widespread use of current interventions, most notably tobacco control.
source_text: Altering the future cost curve for adult survival will require more widespread use of current interventions, most notably tobacco control
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' policy recommendation based on their findings.

claim: Altering the future cost curve for adult survival will require research to identify practicable low-cost drugs, diagnostics, and strategies.
source_text: but also research to identify practicable low-cost drugs, diagnostics, and strategies.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' policy recommendation based on their findings.

claim: Less daily income is required to achieve a certain life expectancy level now compared to the past.
source_text: Life expectancy has continued to increase globally, and this has led to the belief that less daily income is required to achieve a certain life expectancy level
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Casabonne and Kenny (2012).

claim: The majority of gains in life expectancy for low- and middle-income countries have been achieved through reductions in child mortality.
source_text: In this article, we argue that the majority of gains in life expectancy for low- and middle-income countries have been achieved through reductions in child mortality
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' main argument supported by their analysis.

claim: Improvements in adult mortality have been restricted mostly to high-income countries.
source_text: while improvements in adult mortality have been restricted mostly to high-income countries.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' main argument supported by their analysis.

claim: The trends in child and adult mortality have reduced inequality between countries for child survival.
source_text: This has reduced inequality between countries for child survival
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of the declining critical income for children.

claim: The trends in child and adult mortality have increased inequality for adult survival.
source_text: however, increased inequality for adult survival.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of the rising critical income for adults.

claim: The Preston model explains the majority of the observed variance in life expectancy.
source_text: The Preston model explains the majority of the observed variance in life expectancy
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about the Preston model's explanatory power.

claim: The coefficients of the Preston model are not interpretable as no meaning exists for each coefficient nor is a theoretical relationship between them stipulated.
source_text: but the coefficients ('a' and 'b') are not interpretable as no meaning exists for each coefficient nor is a theoretical relationship between them stipulated.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' critique of the Preston model's limitations.

claim: The inadequacy of the Preston models to methodologically identify a single point (such as an inflection point) has led to greater emphasis on the upward rise in the Preston curve, and less attention is devoted to lateral movements.
source_text: The inadequacy of the Preston models to methodologically identify a single point (such as an inflection point; Rogers and Crimmins, 2011), which describes the changing curvature at lower income levels, has led to greater emphasis on the upward rise in the Preston curve, and less attention is devoted to lateral movements (along the income axis).
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' critique supported by reference to Rogers and Crimmins (2011).

claim: Nonparametric regressions have been used to identify a 'hinge' on the Preston curve.
source_text: Nonparametric regressions have been used to identify a 'hinge' on the Preston curve
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Deaton and Case (2009).

claim: No known study has explicitly quantified shifts across income levels in the Preston curve.
source_text: however, we know of no known study that has explicitly quantified shifts across income levels.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' claim about the novelty of their approach based on their literature review.

claim: Infrastructure (such as water sanitation and education systems), vaccinations (leading to long-term immunity), and public health knowledge can be viewed as catalysts that are not consumed in entirety during the process.
source_text: Indeed, infrastructure (such as water sanitation and education systems), vaccinations (leading to long-term immunity), and public health knowledge can be viewed as catalysts that are not consumed in entirety during the process.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' conceptual reasoning for their analogy to catalysts.

claim: The asymptotic leveling of life expectancy at high income seen in the Preston or MM curves is analogous to the saturation of enzymatic sites at high substrate concentration.
source_text: The asymptotic leveling of life expectancy at high income seen in the Preston or MM curves is analogous to the saturation of enzymatic sites at high substrate concentration
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' conceptual analogy between the MM model and mortality patterns.

claim: Further increases in GDP leads to only marginal increases in life expectancy at high income levels.
source_text: thus, further increases in GDP leads to only marginal increases in life expectancy.
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of the asymptotic behavior observed in the data.

claim: The MM model establishes a systematic and empirical method for monitoring not only previously documented upward rises in the Preston curve but also potential shifts along the income axis.
source_text: This model establishes a systematic and empirical method for monitoring not only previously documented upward rises in the Preston curve but also potential shifts along the income axis.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' claim about the methodological advantage of their approach.

claim: An upward rise in the Preston curve can increase the maximum achievable survival for all countries.
source_text: Whereas an upward rise can increase the maximum achievable survival for all countries
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of what an upward shift means.

claim: Lateral shifts in the Preston curve indicate an increase or decrease of income required to achieve maximum survival.
source_text: lateral shifts indicate an increase or decrease of income required to achieve this survival.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of what lateral shifts mean.

claim: Lateral shifts are particularly significant for more resource-limited countries that have yet to reach asymptotic leveling in the health and income relationship.
source_text: These lateral shifts are particularly significant for more resource-limited countries that have yet to reach asymptotic leveling in the health and income relationship.
evidence_reasoning: This is the authors' interpretation of the policy significance of lateral shifts.

claim: Child mortality rate is defined as the probability of a child born in a specific year dying before reaching the age of 5 years, referred to as 5q0.
source_text: Age-specific contributions to changes in life expectancy are quantified using child mortality rate as the probability of a child born in a specific year dying before reaching the age of 5 years, referred to as 5q0
evidence_reasoning: This is a standard demographic definition.

claim: Adult mortality rate represents the probability (for a given year) that an individual who has just turned 15 years will not reach the age of 60 years, referred to as 45q15.
source_text: and the gender-specific adult mortality rate, representing the probability (for a given year) that an individual who has just turned 15 years will not reach the age of 60 years, referred to as 45q15.
evidence_reasoning: This is a standard demographic definition.

claim: A mortality rate of 5 per 1000 corresponds to a 99.5% survival rate.
source_text: We transform these values to survival rates, where a mortality rate of 5 per 1000 corresponds to a 99.5% survival rate.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mathematical transformation between mortality and survival rates.

claim: HIV/AIDS and smoking are two large and widespread public health factors that have influenced mortality over the last four decades.
source_text: Two large and widespread public health factors that have influenced mortality over the last four decades have been the HIV/AIDS pandemic and smoking
evidence_reasoning: This is established public health knowledge.

claim: Smoking makes more common most vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases as well as tuberculosis.
source_text: which makes more common most vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases as well as tuberculosis
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to Gajalakshmi et al. (2003) and Jha (2009).

claim: The study tests if adjustment for the marked heterogeneity of HIV prevalence and cigarette consumption make less efficient the relationship between GDP per capita and adult mortality.
source_text: We test if adjustment for the marked heterogeneity of HIV prevalence (between the ages of 15 and 49 years, as proxy for general population infection levels) and cigarette consumption (at ages 15 years or older) make less efficient the relationship between GDP per capita and adult mortality—as indicated by critical income values.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the hypothesis tested in the covariate analysis.

claim: For the log-linear function, the parameter 'a' was not statistically significant for any year from 1970 to 2000 when using annual income.
source_text: In addition, when using annual income (rather than daily income), the parameter 'a' was not statistically significant for any year from 1970 to 2000.
evidence_reasoning: This is a specific finding from the authors' analysis of the log-linear model.

claim: For children, the critical income values declined gradually from 1970 to 1990, with a large drop in 1990–1995.
source_text: For children, the critical income values declined gradually, however, with a large drop in 1990–1995.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the temporal pattern observed in child critical income.
